#1
L: Thus ever-disciplined, who devotees attend-upon you; and-who also the-imperishable, the-unmanifest — of-them, who [are] the-best-knowers-of-yoga?
I: Those devotees who, ever disciplined in this way, worship you, and those who also worship the imperishable, the unmanifest — which of these know yoga best?
N: Arjuna opens the chapter with the question left hanging since chapter 8: is it better to worship Kṛṣṇa in his personal form, or the impersonal, unmanifest akṣara? The verse is built as a relative-correlative pair, ye ... teṣām, 'those who ... of them' — a construction this chapter uses repeatedly — with the verb paryupāsate, 'they worship, attend upon', supplied in line 1 and understood again in line 2. Sandhi: bhaktās tvāṃ is bhaktāḥ + tvām (-āḥ + t- → -ās t-); cāpy akṣaram is ca + api + akṣaram (ca+api→cāpi, a+a→ā; api+akṣaram→apyakṣaram, -i+a-→-y a-).
#2
L: On-me, having-fixed the-mind, who me constantly-disciplined worship, with faith supreme endowed — they by-me [as] most-disciplined [are] held.
I: Those who fix their mind on me and worship me, ever disciplined and endowed with supreme faith — these I hold to be the most disciplined.
N: The Blessed Lord answers Arjuna's question directly, at least for now: those who fix the mind on him personally (mayi āveśya manaḥ) he calls yuktatamāḥ, 'most disciplined' — though the chapter goes on to qualify this at length. Sandhi: mayy āveśya is mayi + āveśya (-i+ā-→-y ā-), a glide-formation pattern that recurs through the chapter whenever mayi meets a following vowel; nityayuktā upāsate shows a final -āḥ simply dropping before a vowel, with no trace and no avagraha (contrast the -aḥ+a-→-o' pattern, reserved for a following short a-); parayopetās te packs parayā+upetāḥ (-ā+u-→-o-) and upetāḥ+te (-āḥ+t-→-ās t-).
#3
L: But-who the-imperishable, the-indefinable, the-unmanifest attend-upon — all-pervading and-inconceivable, and standing-at-the-peak, unmoving, fixed:
I: But those who instead worship the imperishable, the indefinable, the unmanifest — all-pervading, inconceivable, unchanging, unmoving, eternal —
N: This completes the second alternative of verse 1's question with a stack of near-synonyms for the impersonal absolute, all agreeing with akṣaram: anirdeśya 'indefinable', avyakta 'unmanifest', sarvatra-ga 'going everywhere', acintya 'inconceivable', kūṭa-stha 'standing unchanging at the peak' (kūṭa properly 'summit', used of what stays fixed while all else moves), acala 'unmoving', dhruva 'constant'. The verse and the next form one sentence; the main verb, te prāpnuvanti, comes only in verse 4. Sandhi: tv akṣaram is tu + akṣaram (-u+a-→-v a-, the first instance in this chapter of u fusing to a glide before a vowel); sarvatragam acintyaṃ and kūṭastham acalaṃ are simply pairs of words written joined, the final -m unchanged before the vowel that follows — the same convention already seen at verse 1's akṣaram avyaktam.
#4
L: Having-fully-restrained the-whole-array-of-the-senses, everywhere even-minded, they attain me alone, in-the-welfare-of-all-beings delighting.
I: Restraining the whole array of the senses, even-minded everywhere and delighting in the welfare of all beings, they attain me alone.
N: The sentence begun in verse 3 concludes on the poem's recurring reassurance (cf. 6.31, 9.29) that the personal and impersonal paths arrive at the very same goal: te prāpnuvanti mām eva, 'they attain me, and none other'. Saṃniyamyendriyagrāmam and sarva-bhūta-hite ratāḥ describe the akṣara-worshippers' discipline, in effect a portrait matching the bhaktas described in verses 6-7. Sandhi: saṃniyamyendriyagrāmaṃ is saṃniyamya + indriya-grāmam (-a+i-→-e-); māmeva is mām + eva, simply written together with no phonetic change.
#5
L: Trouble greater [is] for-them whose-minds-are-attached-to-the-unmanifest; the-unmanifest indeed [as] a-goal, with-difficulty, by-embodied-beings is-attained.
I: For those whose minds cling to the unmanifest, the trouble is greater; the unmanifest goal is reached only with difficulty by those who live in a body.
N: Having shown that both paths reach the same end, Kṛṣṇa now weighs their difficulty and finds the impersonal one harder: kleśaḥ adhikataraḥ, 'the trouble is greater', for avyaktāsakta-cetasām, 'those whose minds are fixed on the unmanifest' — not wrong, only harder for an embodied being (deha-vat, 'possessing a body') to sustain, since it gives the mind no form to hold onto. This sets up the easier path urged from verse 6 on. The whole first line is written as one unbroken string: kleśo'dhikatarasteṣāmavyaktāsaktacetasām packs kleśaḥ+adhikataraḥ (-aḥ+a-→-o' with avagraha), adhikataraḥ+teṣām (-aḥ+t-→-as t-), and avyakta+āsakta fusing inside the compound (-a+ā-→-ā-). Gatir duḥkhaṃ and dehavadbhir avāpyate both show a final -iḥ becoming -ir before the next word.
#6
L: But-who all actions in-me having-entrusted, intent-on-me, by-undivided yoga alone meditating, worship [me]:
I: But those who entrust all their actions to me, intent on me as their highest goal, and, meditating on me with undivided yoga, worship me —
N: Kṛṣṇa now describes the easier, personal path: karmāṇi mayi saṃnyasya, 'having laid down all actions in me' (anticipating the surrender taught in chapter 18), mat-parāḥ, 'intent on me', dhyāyantaḥ upāsate, 'meditating, they worship' — a chain of descriptions completed only in verse 7's promise. Ananyena eva yogena, 'by undivided yoga alone', is the poem's constant insistence on singleness of devotion (cf. ananya-cetāḥ at 8.14). Sandhi: ananyenaiva is ananyena + eva (-a+e-→-ai-); dhyāyanta upāsate shows the final -aḥ of the participle silently dropping before the vowel u- — the first clear instance in this chapter of the pattern already at work, unmarked, in verse 2's nityayuktā.
#7
L: Of-them I [am] the-deliverer from-the-ocean-of-death-and-transmigration, I become before-long, O son of Pṛthā, of-those-whose-minds-are-fixed-on-me.
I: For them I quickly become the deliverer from the ocean of death and rebirth, Pārtha — for those whose minds are fixed on me.
N: The promised result of verse 6: Kṛṣṇa himself becomes their samuddhartā, 'rescuer', from mṛtyu-saṃsāra-sāgarāt, 'the ocean of death and transmigration' — one of the poem's several ocean-of-saṃsāra images (cf. 4.36's jñāna-plava, 'raft of knowledge'). Na cirāt, 'not after a long time', i.e. soon, deliberately answers verse 5's warning that the impersonal path is slow. Pārtha, 'son of Pṛthā' (Kuntī), addresses Arjuna. Sandhi: mayy āveśita- is mayi + āveśita (-i+ā-→-y ā-), the glide pattern already seen at verse 2's mayy āveśya.
#8
L: On-me alone the-mind fix, in-me the-understanding place; you-will-dwell in-me alone thereafter — no doubt.
I: Fix your mind on me alone, place your understanding in me; from then on you will dwell in me alone — of this there is no doubt.
N: Two parallel imperatives, ādhatsva and niveśaya, open the practical instruction that runs through verse 12, moving from this hardest ideal (mind wholly fixed on Kṛṣṇa) down through progressively easier alternatives for one who cannot manage it. Mayy eva, 'in me alone', frames both halves of the verse; ataḥ ūrdhvam, 'from this point on', means after death. Sandhi: mana ādhatsva shows the same silent visarga-drop before a vowel as verse 6's dhyāyanta upāsate, here before ā- rather than u-; mayy eva is mayi + eva (-i+e-→-y e-); ata ūrdhvam again drops its visarga silently, this time before ū-.
#9
L: But-if the-mind to-fix-firmly you-are-not-able, steadily, on-me — then, by-the-yoga-of-practice, desire to-attain me, O Winner-of-wealth.
I: But if you cannot steady your mind firmly on me, then seek to reach me through the yoga of repeated practice, Dhanaṃjaya.
N: The first step down from verse 8's ideal: if the mind cannot be held motionless on Kṛṣṇa (samādhātum ... sthiram), the next resort is abhyāsa-yoga, 'the yoga of repeated practice' — patient, habitual effort rather than achieved stillness. Icchāptum packs iccha, the imperative of iṣ 'to wish' ('desire!'), with the infinitive āptum 'to attain' (-a+ā-→-ā-): 'desire to attain [me]'. Dhanaṃjaya, 'winner of wealth' (won in the plunder of conquered kings), is a recurring epithet of Arjuna (cf. 1.15, 4.41, 7.7, 9.9). Sandhi: tato is tataḥ, -aḥ before m- → -o.
#10
L: If-in-practice too incapable you-are, be one-for-whom-action-for-me-is-supreme; for-my-sake even actions performing, perfection you-will-attain.
I: If you are unable even for that practice, be intent on action done for my sake; performing actions for my sake, you will attain perfection.
N: A second step down: if even abhyāsa-yoga is out of reach, the instruction becomes mat-karma-paramaḥ bhava, 'be one for whom action done for me is supreme' — ordinary karma-yoga redirected toward Kṛṣṇa, the same teaching found in chapters 3 and 9. Mad-artham api karmāṇi kurvan, 'even performing actions for my sake', promises siddhim, 'success, accomplishment' — the same word chapter 18 uses technically for the goal of disciplined action. Sandhi: the first line strings three visarga-elisions together — abhyāse'py asamartho'si packs abhyāse+api (-e+a-→-e' with avagraha), api+asamarthaḥ (-i+a-→-y a-), and asamarthaḥ+asi (-aḥ+a-→-o' with avagraha); mat-karma-paramo is mat-karma-paramaḥ, -aḥ before bh- → -o.
#11
L: But-if this too you-are-unable to-do, resorting-to-my-yoga, then the-relinquishment-of-the-fruit-of-all-action do, self-controlled.
I: And if you cannot manage even this, resorting to the yoga directed toward me, then give up the fruit of all action, with your self mastered.
N: The third and last step down before verse 12's summary ranking: mad-yogam āśritaḥ, 'taking refuge in discipline directed toward me' (still oriented to Kṛṣṇa, unlike ordinary renunciation), give up sarva-karma-phala-tyāgam, 'the fruit of all action' — the very teaching of 2.47, offered here as the fallback for one who cannot even perform action as an offering. Yata-ātmavān, 'self-controlled', echoes the self-mastery demanded throughout the chapter. Sandhi: athaitad apy aśakto'si is the densest line so far, packing atha+etat (-a+e-→-ai-), etat+api (-t+a-→-d a-), api+aśaktaḥ (-i+a-→-y a-), and aśaktaḥ+asi (-aḥ+a-→-o' with avagraha) into one breath.
#12
L: Better indeed [is] knowledge than-practice; than-knowledge meditation is-superior; than-meditation the-relinquishment-of-the-fruit-of-action; from-relinquishment peace immediately-follows.
I: Knowledge is better than mere practice; meditation is superior to knowledge; better than meditation is giving up the fruit of action; from that giving-up, peace follows at once.
N: A ranked ladder packed into a single verse, each stage bettering the last: abhyāsa (mechanical practice) < jñāna (knowledge) < dhyāna (meditation) < karma-phala-tyāga (relinquishing the fruit of action) → śānti (peace), reached anantaram, 'immediately'. This is not a contradiction of the descending steps of verses 8-11 but their summary read from the top down. Sandhi runs through both lines: abhyāsāj jñānāt is abhyāsāt+jñānāt (-t+j-→-j j-); jñānād dhyānaṃ is jñānāt+dhyānam (-t+dh-→-d dh-); tyāgas tyāgāt is tyāgaḥ+tyāgāt (-aḥ+t-→-as t-); tyāgācchāntir is tyāgāt+śāntiḥ (-t+ś-→-c ch-, a new assimilation, not yet seen this chapter), followed by the now-familiar -iḥ+a-→-ir a- before anantaram.
#13
L: Not-hating of-all-beings, friendly and compassionate, without-'mine', without-egoism, the-same-in-pain-and-pleasure, forbearing;
I: Free from hatred toward all beings, friendly and compassionate, without possessiveness or egoism, the same in pain and pleasure, forbearing;
N: Kṛṣṇa turns from the ladder of practice to a portrait of the ideal devotee, a string of qualities running through verse 19, each stretch ending in the refrain sa me priyaḥ, 'he is dear to me' (first at v.14). Nirmama and nirahaṃkāra name the twin roots of bondage the poem attacks throughout — 'mine' and 'I' — and sama-duḥkha-sukhaḥ recalls the touchstone of equanimity set at 2.15. This whole verse is a string of nominative adjectives describing one still-unnamed subject; the subject's identity (the devotee) and the main verb arrive only in verse 14. Sandhi: karuṇa eva shows the -aḥ silently dropping before the vowel e-, as already seen at verses 8's ata ūrdhvam; nirmamo is nirmamaḥ, -aḥ before n- → -o.
#14
L: Content, constantly, the-disciplined-one, self-controlled, of-firm-resolve, whose-mind-and-understanding-are-fixed-on-me — who my-devotee [is], he to-me [is] dear.
I: Content, always disciplined, self-controlled, of firm resolve, mind and understanding fixed on me — whoever is my devotee in this way is dear to me.
N: The list from verse 13 continues and the first refrain arrives: yo mad-bhaktaḥ, sa me priyaḥ, 'whoever is my devotee, he is dear to me' — the frame (yaḥ ... saḥ) that shapes verses 14-17, this exact refrain (with small variations) closing verses 14, 16 and 17; verses 18-19 continue the devotee-portrait without repeating the frame, resolving instead at verse 19's naraḥ, and the whole sequence returns, intensified, at 19-20. Mayy arpita-manaḥ-buddhiḥ, 'whose mind and understanding are offered up in me', gives bhakti concrete content here: not feeling alone but the placing of the inner faculties themselves in Kṛṣṇa. Sandhi: mayy arpita- is mayi + arpita (-i+a-→-y a-); manobuddhir yo packs manaḥ+buddhiḥ (-aḥ+b-→-o) and buddhiḥ+yaḥ (-iḥ+y-→-ir y-).
#15
L: From-whom not-is-disturbed the-world, and-who from-the-world is-not-disturbed, and-who by-joy-resentment-fear-and-agitation [is] freed — he too to-me [is] dear.
I: He from whom the world does not shrink, and who does not shrink from the world, and who is free of elation, resentment, fear and anxiety — he too is dear to me.
N: A mutual, reciprocal ease with the world — yasmāt na udvijate lokaḥ, 'the world is not disturbed by him', lokāt na udvijate ca yaḥ, 'and he is not disturbed by the world' — followed by freedom from the four ordinary agitations: harṣa (elation), amarṣa (impatience or resentment), bhaya (fear), udvega (anxiety). Sandhi: yasmānnodvijate and lokānnodvijate both show -t+n-→-n n- followed by na+udvijate fusing to nodvijate (-a+u-→-o-, the same fusion twice); harṣāmarṣabhayodvegair muktaḥ strings two vowel-fusions inside the dvandva compound (-a+a-→-ā-, -a+u-→-o-) before the instrumental plural's visarga elides before m- (-aiḥ+m-→-air m-); mukto yaḥ shows the familiar -aḥ before y- → -o.
#16
L: Without-expectation, pure, capable, indifferent, free-from-distress, one-who-has-relinquished-every-undertaking — who my-devotee [is], he to-me [is] dear.
I: Free from expectation, pure, capable, unconcerned, past all distress, having given up every selfish undertaking — whoever is my devotee like this is dear to me.
N: The list resumes and the refrain repeats. Sarva-ārambha-parityāgī, 'one who has given up every undertaking', does not contradict the poem's earlier insistence on continued action (ch.3): the tradition reads ārambha here as self-interested new projects, not all activity as such. Sandhi: śucir dakṣa udāsīno strings three words together — śuciḥ+dakṣaḥ (-iḥ+d-→-ir d-), dakṣaḥ silently losing its visarga before the vowel u- (as at verse 6's dhyāyanta upāsate), and udāsīnaḥ+gata- (-aḥ before g- → -o); sarvārambha- is sarva+ārambha (-a+ā-→-ā-); yo mad-bhaktaḥ is yaḥ+mad-bhaktaḥ, -aḥ before m- → -o.
#17
L: Who not rejoices, not hates, not grieves, not desires, one-who-has-relinquished-both-good-and-bad — who [has] devotion, he to-me [is] dear.
I: One who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires, who has let go of both good and bad fortune alike — whoever has such devotion is dear to me.
N: A verse of four flat negations (na hṛṣyati, na dveṣṭi, na śocati, na kāṅkṣati) describing equanimity toward whatever comes, followed by śubhāśubha-parityāgī, 'one who has renounced [attachment to] both good and bad' (echoing 2.38's samaḥ labhālabhau). This is the chapter's first bare use of bhaktimān, 'possessing bhakti, devoted' — bhakti itself, translated throughout this chapter (as since chapters 7 and 9) as 'devotion', now appearing on its own rather than only inside the compound mad-bhaktaḥ. Sandhi: yo na is yaḥ+na, -aḥ before n- → -o; śubhāśubha- is śubha+aśubha, -a+a-→-ā-.
#18
L: The-same toward-an-enemy and toward-a-friend, likewise in-honor-and-dishonor; in-cold-and-heat, pleasure-and-pain, the-same, free-from-attachment;
I: The same toward enemy and friend, and likewise in honor and dishonor; the same in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, free from attachment;
N: The chapter's one real vulgate/BORI variant falls here: this text reads mānāpamānayoḥ, 'in honor and dishonor' (apamāna), while the BORI critical edition reads mānāvamānayoḥ, 'in honor and disrespect' (avamāna, a near-synonym also meaning 'dishonor, disrespect'); the sense is essentially unchanged, and the vulgate reading is what is translated here. The verse continues the equanimity-list toward opposite pairs — enemy/friend, honor/dishonor, cold/heat, pleasure/pain — the standard set the poem returns to at 2.14-15, 6.7 and 14.24-25. Sandhi: mānāpamānayoḥ is māna+apamānayoḥ (-a+a-→-ā-); śītoṣṇa- is śīta+uṣṇa (-a+u-→-o-).
#19
L: To-whom-blame-and-praise-are-equal, silent, content with-whatever [comes], homeless, steady-minded, devoted — to-me dear [is that] man.
I: Indifferent to blame and praise, silent, content with whatever comes, without a fixed home, steady-minded and devoted — such a man is dear to me.
N: The last of the devotee-portraits before the summary of verse 20, and the first to name its subject openly as naraḥ, 'the man', rather than leaving him to a bare relative pronoun. Yena kenacit santuṣṭaḥ, 'content with whatever, by whatever [comes]', is an idiom for contentment regardless of circumstance; aniketaḥ, 'without a fixed dwelling', suggests the wandering ascetic's detachment from possessions more than literal homelessness. Sandhi: stutir maunī is stutiḥ+maunī (-iḥ+m-→-ir m-); santuṣṭo is santuṣṭaḥ, -aḥ before y- → -o; sthiramatir bhaktimān is sthiramatiḥ+bhaktimān (-iḥ+bh-→-ir bh-); priyo naraḥ is priyaḥ+naraḥ, -aḥ before n- → -o.
#20
L: But-who this nectar-of-dharma, as-has-been-said, attend-upon, having-faith, having-me-as-their-highest-goal — those devotees exceedingly to-me [are] dear.
I: But those who, full of faith, attend on this nectar of dharma as it has been taught, holding me as their highest goal — such devotees are exceedingly dear to me.
N: The chapter's closing summary gathers everything into one sentence and ends on its key word, priyāḥ, 'dear' — echoing and outdoing the refrain of verses 14-19 (there merely priyaḥ, 'dear', now atīva priyāḥ, 'exceedingly dear'). Dharmyāmṛtam idam, 'this nectar in accord with dharma', names the whole preceding teaching (yathā uktam, 'as it has been stated') as a kind of ambrosia — an image the poem uses elsewhere for a teaching that grants freedom from death. Sandhi: dharmyāmṛtam is dharmya+amṛtam (-a+a-→-ā-); yathoktaṃ is yathā+uktam (-ā+u-→-o-); bhaktās te'tīva packs bhaktāḥ+te (-āḥ+t-→-ās t-) and te+atīva (-e+a-→-e' with avagraha).
